newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK's Railtrack sets investment plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK's Railtrack sets investment plan.

text.p: Railtrack Plc marked its first birthday in the private sector on Tuesday by unwrapping details of a one billion pound ($1.6 billion) spending plan to upgrade 2,500 stations across Britain which it billed as the start of a "rail renaissance".

Sir Robert Horton, chairman of the rail infrastructure firm which inherited billions of pounds in assets when it was privatised 12 months ago, told a press briefing, "Having freed the company from the public sector constraints on spending, Railtrack is set to achieve its vision...to deliver the world's best railway."
The first year as a private company was a sparkling one for investors. Railtrack's shares powered to 426 pence per share from last May's opening price of 225 pence.
Railtrack has outpaced even the dynamic transport sector, outperforming its sector by 84 percent and the FT All Share index by 90 percent since flotation, according to Reuters 3000 data.
But the years ahead may witness a tougher regulatory regime for Railtrack now that the Conservative government which spawned the company has been replaced by a new Labour government.
Labour has pledged more hawkish rail regulation and cited Railtrack's investment track record in particular.
Tuesday's announcement followed a public rebuke from the Rail Regulator, John Swift, last year. The rail watchdog slammed Railtrack's prolonged delays in investment as "wholly unacceptable".
This also triggered threats from Labour's transport team before the election that it could use new legislation to force Railtrack to meet its spending commitments on time.
The move today by the company will ease that tension. But Horton remained unrepentant, saying the delays were justified by preparatory work being done on where to spend the money.
He also denied that the spectre of Labour's windfall tax on privatised utility profits would hamper its spending plans.

"I have no information on the windfall tax or whether it applies to Railtrack," said Horton. "We have provided for this expenditure in our balance sheet and we have made a promise on this. We will spend this money."

He was keeping quiet about the group's views on a possible change in regulation. "It would be silly not to duck the question until I see what form it takes," he said referring to Labour's likely creation of a strategic rail authority with widespread powers.

Passenger groups gave a cautious welcome to the launch of the investment programme. But Save Our Railways added "As we said when Railtrack first announced these plans in February -- it is still lagging way behind the investment planned in Germany and France."
Railtrack says its plans will create a "world class railway". The spending will range from tens of thousands of pounds for a lick of paint to 50 million per station for major redevelopment.
The group has also been working with consultants to develop the "ideal station" of the future -- a new concept with franchises ranging from retailers to medical surgeries.
In future, passengers could buy a dental check-up while waiting for their trains as well as a newspaper or a cup of coffee.
Bob Hill, Railtrack's head of property, said the ideal station would be created out of a "kit of parts" tailored to serve local passenger needs.
He said in future revenues from this type of outlet would be important but would not eclipse Railtrack's true business of generating rail traffic for the network.
"Although we don't benefit from bums on seats. We do benefit from trains on track and we are in the business of encouraging rail usage," said Hill.
While it is Railtrack's job to develop rail traffic, the job of raising passenger numbers lies with the train operating companies which run train services.
($ = 0.608 British Pounds)
